project.objective: When and where did Kenneth Werner Quass die?

questions.question: When and where did Kenneth Werner Quass (born 4 December 1917, Iowa; FamilySearch KNS4-P6W) die?
questions.rationale: The objective is a single event (the death) with two attributes, date and place, so it is restated with identifying detail rather than split. The tree holds no death fact for the subject, and the pre-provided captures (a Texas death certificate and a Find a Grave memorial) are not yet extracted, so no answer is yet on record. The tree also gives conflicting birth places for the subject (Sumner, Bremer per the birth fact; Independence, Buchanan per a family life sketch), which the death search should not depend on. Sources to test: the uploaded Texas death certificate and Find a Grave memorial first, then other death indexes for the period.

items.jurisdiction: Unknown until the capture is read (file name names Texas; not treated as evidence)
items.rationale: The uploaded file uploads/ancestry-texas-death-cert-quass.pdf has no extracted text in the project, so its contents are unknown to this plan. Its file name names Texas, which is a label only. Extraction must read it before any search is chosen. If it records a date and place of death, the state of death is identified and that state's vital records series becomes the next plan; if not, the remaining items run.

items.jurisdiction: Unknown until the memorial is read (burial place not yet known)
items.repository: Find a Grave (researcher upload, local file)
items.rationale: The uploaded file uploads/findagrave-quass-54602333.pdf has no extracted text in the project. A memorial can state a death date and a burial place, which would answer both parts of the question if the memorial is sourced. Extraction must read it; a memorial alone is a derivative lead to verify against a death record.

United States, Social Security Death Index (collection 1202535) is name-searchable and is the national death index covering the later years of the period. It can give a death date and last residence ZIP, which narrows the state of death. The tree records a move to Los Angeles, California on 2 July 1962, so a death after that date is plausible, but no place of death is implied. A negative result is not evidence that he did not die.

United States, Social Security Numerical Identification Files (NUMIDENT), 1936-2007 (collection 5000016) is name-searchable. Its death-related content is not confirmed by the survey, so this item checks whether it carries a death date or a place of death for the subject. Run alongside the Social Security Death Index, not after it.

United States, Residence Database, 1970-2024 (collection 5000290) and United States, Public Records, 1970-2009 (collection 2199956) are both name-searchable. They can show the subject's last known residence, which is the most likely place of death if no certificate turns up. They do not record a death, so a residence is a lead to a state or county for a death record, not an answer.

United States, Census, 1950 (collection 4464515) is name-searchable and shows the subject alive in 1950. It fixes his residence before the years of likely death and so narrows the state to search. It does not record a death. The 1940 census shows him alive too, and the tree already records his 1940 residence in Madelia, Minnesota, so the 1950 entry is the next residence check.

The FamilySearch obituary collections (United States, Obituary Records, 2014-2023, collection 5000145; GenealogyBank obituary collections 2860782 and 2333694, also indexed on FamilySearch) are name-searchable. An obituary often gives a death date, a place of death and the survivors. It is a derivative lead to verify against a death record. The 2024-2026 period has no obituary collection in the survey, so it is not covered here.

U.S. Find a Grave Index on Ancestry is an index only and paid. It is the fallback if the uploaded memorial in pli_002 cannot be read or does not settle the death date or place. A burial index gives a death date only when the memorial states it, so it is a lead to verify against a death record.

U.S. Deaths and Burials 1867-1961 on FamilySearch is index only. It ends before the years of likely death, since the subject was born in 1917 and may have died later, so a negative result is not evidence he did not die. It is checked only for a death before 1962.

Triage of researcher upload uploads/findagrave-quass-54602333.pdf (Find a Grave memorial 54602333, captured 6/15/26, 3 pages; the URL above is the search that reaches this subject, built after the capture arrived, so the entry closes no in-flight row). Memorial for Kenneth Werner Quass Sr., birth 4 Dec 1917 Buchanan County, Iowa; death given as 17 Sep 1982, Grapevine, Tarrant County, Texas; burial Riverside Cemetery, Madelia, Watonwan County, Minnesota. Compiled, user-contributed source (contributor G R Wise Gittens, memorial added 7 Jul 2010), a lead only. The memorial's own text says the death-certificate place of death is false: the subject reportedly died en route from Miami to San Diego on a commercial airline, was found dead in a lavatory, and the body was unloaded at the Dallas downtown airport, with no autopsy; cause of death is stated as unknown. The informant's account is hearsay from a son who says he resided in Minnesota, and the memorial text itself says the informant's signature was forged on the certificate. Photographed headstones (Kenneth W, Dec 4 1917 - Sept 1982) are images of an artifact, weaker than the text only in what they show. Points to verify: the death certificate itself (state of Texas Vital Records if the place of death is Texas), any airline or coroner record of a death in flight, and the Dallas or Miami airport death. Family links here (parents Ralph Kennedy Quass and Emma Wilhelmina Nehls; spouse Ivyl Phylena Greenley m. 1938; children Donald Wendell and Alice Jeanette) match the project tree. The file name's 54602333 matches the memorial id on the capture.

## Kenneth Werner Quass Sr.

**BIRTH** 4 Dec 1917
Buchanan County, Iowa, USA
**DEATH** 17 Sep 1982 (aged 64)
Grapevine, Tarrant County, Texas, USA
**BURIAL** Riverside Cemetery
Madelia, Watonwan County, Minnesota, USA
**MEMORIAL ID** 54602333

The information on the death certificate as place of death is false. Kenneth Werner died en-route from Miami, Florida to his home in San Diego, California, on a commercial airline. He was found dead in the rear toilet of the plane and his remains were placed in the last seat of the plane covered with a blanket until the plane landed at the downtown Dallas airport. I confirmed this with the airline he was the passenger on to thank them for their respectful treatment of my father's remains. He was dead upon arrival, but the coroner did not do an autopsy as required. He called Ken's son, the author of this bit of information, after talking with Ken's wife and asked some health questions as well as Kenneth W Quass' occupation. Kenneth was a national sales representative for several foreign auto parts manufacturers and was returning home from an extended visit with foreign auto parts suppliers and vehicle repair shops along the east coast of the USA. As a national sales representative, he had many friends and acquaintances in the USA. The coroner glibly put down as Ken's occupation as in 'auto sales' implying not of much importance an never performed an autopsy as federal law requires when one passes on a commercial airline. The coroner simply made an assumption as to the cause of death and noted the place of death as though it happened on the ground in Dallas. He then forged my signature on the death certificate as the informant. I resided in Minnesota at that time. In effect, Ken's cause of death is unknown. At his funeral, a close friend of the family aske me if an autopsy had been performed. I said no,, and he replied you may wish one had been done, for he was well aware of my father's

---

health. A year or so later a Minnesota based foreign auto parts supplier approached me to ask if I knew what my father died of. I said no, He replied if I had ever thought of foul play. He proceeded to offer 'facts' that would support foul play at the Miami airport. I won't go into that with this bit of information, but it proved quite plausible.

conflicts.description: Kenneth Quass (KNS4-P6W) death place, 17 Sep 1982: Grapevine, Tarrant, Texas per the Texas death certificate transcription (a_007) and the Find a Grave header field (a_019), versus a commercial flight from Miami toward San Diego that landed at the downtown Dallas airport, with the body found in a rear toilet, per the memorial narrative (a_020). The memorial narrative says the certificate's place is false.
conflicts.independence_analysis: Two of the three assertions are not independent of each other. a_019 is the Find a Grave header place, and the same memorial's narrative (a_020) explicitly disowns that place, so a_019 adds no separate witness: it repeats the contested certificate place from the same submitted memorial. a_020 and a_019 share the contributor as their only known origin. a_007 comes from a separate source (the Ancestry capture of the Texas death record) and is the only assertion that does not trace to the memorial contributor, so it is the one independent line of evidence. The certificate itself is the underlying record for a_007 and the memorial's header field may simply be copied from it, so even a_007 and a_019 may be one informational chain; the memorial's contributor is the only source for the claim that the certificate is wrong.
conflicts.weighing_analysis: a_007 is an official record created by the certifying official under legal duty, which weighs in favor of its place. It is a transcription, however, and the page image was not checked against the transcription here. a_020 is a later, unsourced narrative by the decedent's son, who says he signed as informant without knowledge, that no autopsy was done, and that cause was undetermined. That is a claim against the official record with a personal motive and no airline, coroner, or flight record behind it. Its specifics (flight route, toilet, Dallas landing) are concrete enough to be checked, and the claim that the coroner recorded a place as if on the ground is itself unverified. Neither side can be set aside on the four defensible rationales yet: the official record is a single source, and the contributor account is a single uncorroborated source, so the conflict turns on evidence not in the file.
conflicts.resolution_rationale: The problem: the place of death for Kenneth Quass in 1982 is disputed. It matters because it determines which jurisdiction's death record and coroner's file to search and whether the death was on the ground at all. The evidence: the Texas death record, captured from Ancestry, gives Grapevine, Tarrant County; the Find a Grave memorial repeats that place in its header, while its narrative, by the decedent's son, says the death occurred on a commercial flight from Miami to San Diego that landed in Dallas. The record favors Grapevine on its face because it is an official record made by a certifying official in the course of duty. The son is the only source for the flight account, is a family member with a motive to dispute the certificate, says he signed as informant without knowing what he was signing, and gives no documentary support. Neither side meets a defensible rationale for setting the other aside, so the conflict stays open. The narrower reason the two accounts diverge may be that a death aboard an aircraft, reported to a Texas county on arrival, would be recorded at the landing point; the coroner's entry could then name Dallas-area or Grapevine jurisdiction without the death having occurred on the ground there. That explanation is a hypothesis, not a finding.

localities.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: United States (national record sets; the place of death is not yet known) (1940-2026)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** the United States is a country; the survey's place record gives a date range from 1776.
- **County seat / administrative center:** not applicable at national level; death records are held by the state and county where the death occurred.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** none (national level).
- **Population during period:** the survey's population figures run from about 132 to 135 million in 1940 to about 349 million in 2026 (projected figure in the survey).
- **Economy:** not covered by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** not covered by this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** the FamilySearch Wiki United States Church Records page covers denominations by state; no denomination was read for this survey.
- **Key historical events:** not covered by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** the volumes part timed out, so no digitized volume counts are reported. The Catalog returned 309,380 national hits, none specific to death records for this period. The external links part returned 1,998 curated links without listing them.

## Boundary changes
- The survey found no national boundary change relevant to death records for 1940-2026.
- Death records follow the state or county where the death occurred, not the national collections. Once the place of death is known, check that state's jurisdiction as a separate locality guide.
- The FamilySearch Wiki United States Genealogy page states that genealogy records are kept at the state level in the United States.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** First, search the FamilySearch Social Security Death Index (collection 1202535, 1875-2014), which is free and covers the later years of the period. Second, search the Social Security NUMIDENT (collection 5000016) and the Obituary Records (collection 5000145) for a date and residence. Third, identify the state of death and request its death certificate from the state's Vital Records office. The Wiki's national death indexes (1867-1961 on FamilySearch; 1833-1970 on Findmypast) end before the likely death years.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's United States Online Genealogy Records page lists national death indexes and cemetery indexes; the [United States Online Genealogy Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Online_Genealogy_Records) page is the source for the index dates above.
- The [United States Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Research_Tips_and_Strategies) page advises that a death record often gives parents' names; the 1940 and 1950 census can show residence before death.
- Alternative sources when the death record is not found: obituaries (GenealogyBank collections 2860782 and 2333694), cemetery indexes (Find a Grave, paid, on Ancestry), and the Veterans' Gravesites index if the subject served in the military.
- The survey did not read the state Vital Records pages, the county probate pages, or the Find a Grave and Texas death certificate uploads for this subject. The place of death is unresolved, so the next step is to read the uploaded leads and then the matching state's death-record series.
